views.prompt: Create an independent research-guided scientific hypothetical illustration of a very low camera view above an imagined local surface of asteroid (10) Hygiea. Landscape 16:9. Subdued neutral dark grey regolith with gently rolling low relief, scattered modest irregular stones and fine grains, a few shallow small depressions, restrained oblique lighting and a black sky. No visible astronomical disks, spacecraft, people, buildings, atmosphere or active phenomena. Invent every local feature independently; do not copy any real body map or observed planetary photograph. Neither native SPHERE brightness patterns nor fitted ADAM facets are local terrain templates. Chemistry, grain size, porosity, colour, horizon attitude, illumination and exposure are unmeasured artistic choices. Add a simple dark footer with two crisp readable lines: "IMAGINED LOCAL VIEW — (10) HYGIEA" and "INVENTED TERRAIN / COLOUR / LIGHT — NO REGISTERED SITE". Do not portray a survivable human landing.

Create a second independent scientific hypothetical observer illustration looking along a different imagined horizon of asteroid (10) Hygiea, landscape 16:9. Show only a low strip of dark neutral grey invented regolith and a few independent angular stones beneath an expansive black sky. The Sun stays entirely outside the frame; no planets, moons, stars as disks, spacecraft, people or artificial structures. Use restrained low side light and a visibly different composition from the local view. All relief, rocks, grain size, chemistry, colour, attitude, light and exposure are invented; black sky is an artistic assumption and is not evidence about atmosphere. Do not borrow any observed asteroid or planetary map or SPHERE image brightness pattern. No dated or physically registered viewpoint and no angular-size claim. Add a crisp readable two-line dark footer: "IMAGINED SKY FROM (10) HYGIEA" and "UNREGISTERED VIEW / INVENTED TERRAIN, COLOUR AND LIGHT". No active plume, exposed ocean, biology or survivable landing.

fields.text: A new SPHERE/VLT image of Hygiea, which could be the Solar System’s smallest dwarf planet yet. As an object in the main asteroid belt, Hygiea satisfies right away three of the four requirements to be classified as a dwarf planet: it orbits around the Sun, it is not a moon and, unlike a planet, it has not cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit. The final requirement is that it have enough mass that its own gravity pulls it into a roughly spherical shape. This is what VLT observations have now revealed about Hygiea.
